https://www.hngn.com/articles/273179/202.text: A suspected Russian drone came close to striking Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's aircraft as it prepared to depart Moldova on Monday, an incident that forced the closure of Moldovan airspace, sent NATO fighter jets into the air over Romania, and was disclosed only the following day by Norway's prime minister — raising a question that neither Kyiv nor its partners have answered publicly: whether the drone's timing was coincidence or something else. "His flight was almost hit by a drone when it was taking off from Moldova. That is the reality he lives in," Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre told Norwegian broadcaster NRK on Tuesday, after Zelensky arrived in Oslo ahead of the funeral of King Harald V. A source familiar with the incident separately confirmed the near miss to the Kyiv Independent.The reconstructed timeline shows how narrowly the episode unfolded. Moldova's military first detected an unidentified unmanned aerial vehicle entering the country's airspace at about 4:20 p.m. local time Monday, and authorities closed the airspace shortly after 4:30, delaying three departures and four arrivals at Chisinau International Airport — among them the Ukrainian presidential aircraft. At 4:37 p.m., Romania's Defense Ministry said the drone had crossed into Romanian, and therefore NATO, airspace; two minutes later, two Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed under NATO's enhanced Air Policing mission took off to monitor it. The jets tracked but did not intercept the drone, and Romanian radar lost contact at 5:02 p.m. Five minutes later the drone was detected again over Moldova, where it came down and exploded near Mihailenii Vechi in the Rascani district, roughly 25 kilometers east of the Romanian border and about 160 kilometers from the Chisinau airport. Flight restrictions were lifted after 5:20 p.m. once authorities confirmed the drone was down, and Zelensky's plane took off at approximately 5:57 p.m., later than scheduled. A Moldovan government spokesperson later said two Russian drones had been involved in the incident — one landing in a field north of the capital and sparking a fire, the other continuing into Romanian airspace.The drone's exact type has not been officially established. Ukrainian open-source monitoring channels identified it as a Geran-4, one of Russia's newer jet-powered attack drones — a class of weapon that blurs the line between traditional unmanned aircraft and low-cost cruise missiles, flying faster than the propeller-driven Shahed variants that have defined much of the drone war and proving considerably harder to intercept. Moldova's Defense Ministry described the intruder as a Shahed-type drone in its initial statement, which made no mention of the presidential aircraft. Moldova, which is not a NATO member, has no air-defense system capable of intercepting drone-class threats at scale, and Russian drones and missiles have violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace repeatedly in recent months — a pattern that produced deadly consequences within days of Monday's incident, when a Russian drone strike on the Starokozache border checkpoint between Ukraine and Moldova killed two civilians and closed the crossing.Zelensky's routing itself reflects the security calculus his travel has required since Russia's full-scale invasion began in 2022. For most of the war, the Ukrainian president has traveled abroad primarily overland through Poland, with the airport at Rzeszow serving as his regular departure point; only in recent months has his presidential aircraft begun using Chisinau more frequently for foreign trips, a shift that put Monday's flight path directly beneath the corridor the drone crossed. Neither the Moldovan military nor Ukraine's government has publicly addressed whether the drone posed a deliberate threat to the aircraft, and the Kremlin has consistently denied targeting Ukraine's leadership. But the suspicion that the timing was not accidental has attached itself to the episode regardless, fed by precedents that make such questions unavoidable — among them the August 2023 crash inside Russia of the private jet carrying Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin, two months to the day after his abortive mutiny.The near miss landed at a diplomatically raw moment. It occurred days after President Trump's lead negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, visited Kyiv and Moscow in a peace push that produced little beyond tentative talk of future trilateral meetings, and as Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov was publicly dismissing European ceasefire proposals as attempts to buy Ukraine time. Zelensky's Norway trip — centered on air defense assistance and immediate winter needs alongside the royal funeral — was itself part of Kyiv's response to a war whose air campaign has intensified as its diplomacy has stalled: Ukraine is seeking contracts for roughly 1,000 Patriot interceptor missiles and pursuing a license to manufacture them domestically, requests given fresh urgency by a week in which Russian drones struck a Kyiv television station mid-broadcast and a border post on the edge of NATO's neighborhood.For NATO, the episode adds another entry to a growing file. The alliance's aircraft have scrambled repeatedly this year to track Russian drones straying into Romanian and Polish airspace, and Monday's sequence — a NATO air policing mission monitoring, but not engaging, a Russian attack drone transiting alliance territory while the Ukrainian president's aircraft waited on a tarmac 160 kilometers away — captures the narrow margin on which the current rules of engagement operate. Whether those rules would have looked adequate had the drone come down somewhere other than a field in Rascani district is the question Store's disclosure has now put in front of every government whose airspace sits along the war's western edge.
